newsitem.title: ITALY: Castro watches as second protest hits food summit.
newsitem.headline: Castro watches as second protest hits food summit.

text.p: Protesters ripped up the final declaration of the U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit in front of leaders including Cuban President Fidel Castro on Sunday in the second security breach to disrupt the gathering.
"This is a farce," screamed one young woman as security officials dragged her from the summit's closing news conference at the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO).
"You are presiding over a criminal process," she shouted in English as security officials struggled to silence her and bundled her roughly away by the hair.
The demonstration was the second to be staged inside the FAO headquarters in Rome following a naked protest last Wednesday.
It took place in the same hall where assembled heads of state and government had addressed the summit and was potentially the more serious of the two.
Some 10,000 police were drafted in to guard around 80 leaders and Castro has been escorted by armed bodyguards and a machine-gun toting guard in a jeep outside the summit.
But the handful of demonstrators, who apparently had media accreditation, were able to stand up unchecked within reach of the communist leader on Sunday.
A later news release issued by "The Hunger Gathering" identified the protesters as representing a forum of concerned environmentalists and activist groups.
"Participants at the closing press conference at the World Food Summit were today choking on the words of the FAO," said the statement headed "FAO we cannot eat your words".

"We wanted to show that their words will do nothing to alleviate the hunger and environmental crisis the FAO has helped create," the statement added. "The empty words of the FAO will not feed the starving millions."
The summit has pledged in its main declaration to halve the number of hungry in the world by the year 2015.

Castro and Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina were listening to Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, the summit chairman, open the news conference with a welcome when a young man in a suit and tie stood up in the front row.
As he began to shout, he was joined by two women who began ripping up the final summit declaration and stuffing the shredded paper into their mouths.
One woman referred to transnational corporations and the World Bank. The other, speaking in foreign accented English, yelled: "They're not there to feed the people".

The later statement accused FAO of attempting to silence dissent and "fawning" to a "powerful lobby of exclusively profit-driven transnational corporations and the manouevres of industrialised nations such as the USA".
There was no suggestion that the protest was against Castro, who himself slammed capitalism and consumerism as a cause of hunger in his summit speech on Saturday.
"This is a press conference, not a show," the summit's chief spokeswoman, Karen-Lis Svarre, said from the podium.
Prodi tried to defuse the situation as the conference resumed, commenting to laughter from the hall: "The first part of the news conference was a success.
Police had enforced tougher security for the summit after three women stripped naked on Wednesday at a news conference held by U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman.
That protest was against genetically manipulated soybeans produced by U.S. company Monsanto.
